title: Available for Use (AFU) - Canadian SR&ED Tax Glossary
description: Read our Canadian SR&ED glossary to understand the Available for Use (AFU) rules for depreciable property and tax credits.
summary: Available-for-use (AFU) timing rules determine when Canadian corporations and other SR&ED claimants can claim investment tax credits on restored capital and shared-use equipment acquired after December 15, 2024. Under amended subsection 127(11.2) of the Income Tax Act, ITC eligibility follows AFU timing, while property acquired before December 16, 2024 remains ineligible.

body.text: Available-for-use (AFU) timing rules determine when Canadian corporations and other SR&ED claimants can claim investment tax credits on restored capital and shared-use equipment acquired after December 15, 2024. Under amended subsection 127(11.2) of the Income Tax Act, ITC eligibility follows AFU timing, while property acquired before December 16, 2024 remains ineligible.

Canada's flagship innovation tax regime—the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—is the single largest federal government program supporting R&D in Canada, allowing $4.6 billion in investment tax credits (ITCs) across 23,677 processed claims during the fiscal year from April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026. Between December 2024 and November 2026, Canada's R&D tax architecture underwent its largest statutory and administrative expansion in more than a decade. Enacted on March 26, 2026 through Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), federal law doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million, widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a three-year average gross revenue phase-out, permitted Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) to elect into that gross revenue formula, and restored SR&ED deductibility and ITC eligibility for capital expenditures and equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024.

Concurrent administrative, budgetary, and provincial reforms have further reshaped R&D compliance strategy across Canada. On April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process offering upfront project eligibility decisions within eight weeks for businesses with less than $25 million in gross business income. On November 5, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 tabled a new wave of legislative proposals—applicable, according to PwC Canada's budget analysis, to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 pending parliamentary enactment—to bring commercialization regulatory testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs directly inside the SR&ED regime rather than creating a standalone patent box, while eliminating certified board resolution filing requirements for corporate SR&ED elections upon Royal Assent. Provincially, Québec replaced its legacy R&D wage and partnership tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 with the refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), offering 30% on up to $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter. Ontario simultaneously aligned its capital expenditure rules with federal post-December 15, 2024 restoration while preserving its $3 million expenditure limit on the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC).
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2025–2026 Reform Cycle
1.1 Statutory Foundations in the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal SR&ED program operates under a dual institutional structure: the Department of Finance Canada formulates legislative tax policy and statutory amendments, while the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers technical and financial claim reviews, publishes binding administrative forms and interpretive policies, and assesses tax returns. Unlike competitive innovation grants, SR&ED incentives are non-discretionary statutory entitlements codified in the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the Act), and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations (the Regulations). Any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada whose research or development work and related expenditures satisfy the statutory tests and mandatory filing deadlines is entitled by law to the resulting income deductions and tax credits.
Five core statutory pillars of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations govern every federal SR&ED claim:

items: Definitional Scope — Subsection 248(1) of the Act: Subsection 248(1) establishes the controlling legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development", delineating eligible basic research, applied research, experimental development, commensurate support work, and excluded commercial or routine activities. (A former definition inside section 37 was repealed under S.C. 1996, c. 21, s. 9(8) to consolidate statutory interpretation in subsection 248(1)). Subsection 248(1) also defines "salary or wages", establishing the employment-income baseline for eligible payroll claims.

Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool — Section 37 of the Act: Subsection 37(1) establishes a cumulative expenditure pool permitting taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada to deduct allowable current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and, following post-December 15, 2024 restoration, eligible capital SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) against business income in the year incurred or carry unclaimed pool balances forward to future taxation years. Section 37 extends territorial scope to Canada's exclusive economic zone (including the airspace above and seabed or subsoil below that zone) within the meaning of the Oceans Act, while subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) cap permissible direct-employee SR&ED salaries incurred outside Canada at 10% of directly engaged Canadian SR&ED salaries, and subsection 37(2) governs payments to approved institutions for research outside Canada. Paragraph 37(1)(d) reduces the deductible pool by government and non-government assistance; subsection 37(4) bars deductions for expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED; subsection 37(8) defines directly attributable current, capital, and lease expenditures; subsection 37(11) establishes the strict statutory filing deadline for prescribed Form T661; and section 37 deems work performed for a non-arm's-length person or partnership to be SR&ED where the work would have qualified had that party performed it directly.

Investment Tax Credit Computation and Expenditure Limits — Section 127 of the Act: Subsection 127(5) governs the application of SR&ED ITCs against Part I federal tax otherwise payable, including three-year carryback and twenty-year carryforward rules. Subsection 127(8) governs partnership ITC allocations. Subsection 127(9) defines "investment tax credit", "qualified expenditure", "contract payment", and "eligible Canadian public corporation", and includes paragraph 127(9)(m), which disqualifies any expenditure from earning an ITC unless the prescribed form containing prescribed information is filed within one year after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year. Subsection 127(10.1) adds the 20% enhanced ITC supplement atop the 15% basic rate (totalling 35%), while subsections 127(10.2), 127(10.21), 127(10.3), 127(10.31), 127(10.32), 127(10.5), and 127(10.6) govern the $6 million expenditure limit, associated-group allocations, short-year proration, and taxable capital versus gross revenue phase-out formulas. Subsections 127(18) to 127(20) mandate reductions to qualified expenditures for assistance and contract payments, and subsections 127(27) to 127(36) govern ITC recapture.

Refundable Investment Tax Credit Mechanics — Section 127.1 of the Act: Subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), 127.1(2.01), and 127.1(3) establish cash refundability for qualifying claimants without sufficient Part I tax payable, deeming refunded ITCs to have been deducted against Part I tax under subsection 127(5) so refunded credits reduce carryover pools dollar-for-dollar. (Auditors reviewing historical provisions of the Act should distinguish active section 127.1 refundability from legacy section 127.3 and Part VIII section 194 provisions, which relate to the historical 1980s scientific research tax credit share/debt designation mechanism).

Prescribed Proxy Amount and Overhead Rules — Section 2900 of the Regulations: Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations governs directly attributable overhead under the traditional method and sets the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4) at 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base, subject to specified employee caps and salary-base exclusions under subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9). Under paragraph 12(1)(x) of the Act, any portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit attributable to the notional PPA must be included in taxable income in the year received.

body.text: 1.2 Enacted Bill C-15 Reforms (Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

From January 1, 2014 through December 15, 2024, Canada's SR&ED program operated under austerity parameters enacted in 2012–2013: the basic ITC rate had dropped from 20% to 15% after 2013, the PPA rate had stepped down from 65% (up to 2012) and 60% (in 2013) to 55% from 2014 onward, arm's-length contractor and third-party payments had been restricted to 80% ITC inclusion after 2012, and capital expenditures and equipment lease outlays had been completely excluded. Beginning in late 2024, the federal government reversed those restrictions through a multi-stage legislative reform.

Auditors verifying 2024–2026 corporate tax filings and financial-statement tax provisions must track the exact legislative chronology, because interim figures proposed in late 2024 were superseded before enactment. In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement tabled on December 16, 2024, the Department of Finance initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, broadening the CCPC taxable capital phase-out corridor to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% refundable credit to ECPCs, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility. On August 15, 2025, the Department of Finance released draft legislative proposals for stakeholder consultation. Subsequently, Budget 2025 raised the proposed annual expenditure limit further—from $4.5 million to $6.0 million—retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. According to a static accrual estimate by the Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO), raising the expenditure cap from $4.5 million to $6.0 million alone reduces federal revenues by $277 million between 2025–2026 and 2029–2030. As documented in accounting firm legislative summaries and CRA announcements, Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) was introduced in Parliament on November 18, 2025, passed third reading in the House of Commons on February 26, 2026, cleared the Senate without amendment, and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 as S.C. 2026, c. 3 (including consequential repeals such as subsection 37(14)).

Bill C-15 enacted two distinct coming-into-force rules that must never be conflated during claim verification. First, the $6.0 million expenditure limit, the $15 million to $75 million taxable capital phase-out thresholds, the extension of the 35% enhanced ITC to ECPCs, and the CCPC election to use the three-year average gross revenue test apply strictly by fiscal period—to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024. Consequently, a corporation with a January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025 taxation year accesses the $6.0 million cap for its entire 2025 return, whereas a corporation whose taxation year began on December 1, 2024 remained governed by the $3.0 million cap until its fiscal year beginning December 1, 2025. Second, the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures and lease costs applies by transaction date—covering depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 and equipment lease costs incurred or first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 (subject to available-for-use timing rules for ITC purposes under amended subsection 127(11.2), as noted in specialist tax bulletins). Any depreciable property acquired before December 16, 2024 remains strictly ineligible for SR&ED deductions or ITCs. (Bill C-15 also enacted technical amendments to Regulations 3100(1)(b) and 3100(3) regarding government assistance and concessional loans for prescribed tax-shelter benefit rules, deemed in force January 1, 2022).
1.3 Proposed Federal Budget 2026 Enhancements (Tabled November 5, 2026)

On November 5, 2026, Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne presented the 2026 Federal Budget. Because these announcements were tabled days prior to this report and await implementing legislation, auditors must treat them as proposed legislative measures rather than enacted law. According to PwC Canada's analysis of the 2026 Federal Budget, Ottawa proposed three targeted expansions and administrative simplifications to the SR&ED program rather than introducing a separate preferential corporate income tax rate ("patent box") on IP income:

First, for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligible SR&ED activities and expenditures to encompass regulatory and certification commercialization work—specifically tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to satisfy regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification needed to commercialize a product or process. All standard SR&ED expenditure categories (salaries and wages, materials, contracting costs, overhead, and machinery and equipment) will be claimable for these qualifying regulatory activities.

Second, also effective for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, Budget 2026 proposes to make costs related to the registration and maintenance of IP protection eligible SR&ED expenditures where the underlying IP was developed during an eligible SR&ED project. Qualifying IP instruments under relevant Canadian or equivalent foreign legislation encompass four statutory classes: patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. To prevent subsidized IP from being transferred out of the Canadian tax base without consequence, if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED support was claimed on IP protection costs, recapture rules will claw back both the related SR&ED deduction and the related ITC.

Third, effective for corporate tax elections and agreements made on or after the date of Royal Assent of the enacting legislation, Budget 2026 proposes to eliminate the requirement for corporations to file certified copies of board resolutions or corporate authorizations when submitting SR&ED elections—specifically transfers of qualified SR&ED contract expenditures (Form T1146) and allocations of specified employee SR&ED salaries (Form T1174)—with a second tranche of corporate tax simplification measures scheduled for the 2027 Spring Economic Update.

body.text: 2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework
2.1 The Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1)

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. To qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, work must be conducted in Canada (or within Canada's exclusive economic zone under the Oceans Act, subject to the limited 10% foreign employee support rule under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)) and fall within one of four statutory work categories:

items: Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as laboratory or theoretical investigations characterizing a newly discovered virus.

Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as investigating biological characteristics of that virus specifically to formulate a candidate vaccine.

Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new, or improve existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements—such as scaling up and optimizing reaction or manufacturing processes where existing technological knowledge cannot predict large-scale behaviour.

Support Work: Work in engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, strictly to the extent that such work directly supports and is commensurate with the needs (in amount, size, extent, and duration) of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development.

body.text: 2.2 CRA's "Why" and "How" Methodology and Project Grouping

Published on August 13, 2021, the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives structure technical reviews around two cumulative requirements: Why the work was conducted (scientific or technological advancement) and How the work was conducted (systematic investigation or search).

The "Why" requirement mandates that the primary purpose of the work be the generation or discovery of new knowledge that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely advancing the claimant's commercial business practices. New scientific or technological knowledge is needed only where scientific or technological uncertainty exists at the outset of the project—meaning it is unknown or uncertain whether a sought result can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency or limitation in the existing scientific or technological knowledge base. Importantly, achieving commercial or technical success is not required: proving through controlled testing that a hypothesized engineering approach cannot overcome a physical or algorithmic constraint still generates new negative technological knowledge and fully qualifies as SR&ED.

The "How" requirement governs execution methodology. Merely adopting an organized engineering workflow or applying established analytical protocols does not constitute a systematic investigation or search. Under CRA eligibility guidelines, the work must execute four sequential steps:

items: Defining a specific scientific or technological problem rooted in a knowledge-base limitation;
Advancing a testable hypothesis toward resolving that problem;
Planning and testing the hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis; and
Developing logical scientific or technological conclusions based on the empirical or analytical results.

body.text: Because businesses organize engineering teams around commercial product roadmaps rather than subsection 248(1) boundaries, the CRA enforces structured project-grouping rules on Part 2 of Form T661. An "SR&ED project" is defined as a set of interrelated activities performed by qualified individuals that collectively attempt to resolve specific scientific or technological uncertainties to achieve a common advancement. An SR&ED project begins when the need for an advancement to overcome a technological uncertainty is identified and ends as soon as that new knowledge is gained, even if commercial engineering continues afterward. Claimants group work under one of three CRA scenarios: grouping an entire business project as one SR&ED project when 100% of its tasks are eligible; carving out only eligible core and commensurate support activities where a business project mixes routine engineering and SR&ED; or aggregating eligible activities across multiple commercial projects into a single SR&ED project where all grouped activities pursue the same underlying technological advancement. While projects frequently span multiple fiscal periods, expenditures may only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are incurred.
2.3 Statutory Exclusions and Non-Qualifying Activities
Subsection 248(1) and CRA eligibility guidance explicitly exclude seven categories of routine, commercial, or non-technological work from SR&ED, even if performed within a broader R&D department:

items: Market research or sales promotion;
Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Research in the social sciences or the humanities;

Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (supported separately through resource tax provisions such as the Mineral Exploration Tax Credit, extended through March 31, 2027 by Bill C-15);

Commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or commercial use of a new or improved process (where experimental trials coincide with commercial runs, the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy isolate incremental experimental runs from excess commercial production);
Style changes; and
Routine data collection.

body.text: In addition, CRA guidelines explicitly disqualify internal capability-building activities that do not advance the underlying scientific or technological knowledge base—specifically employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or outside consultants who already possess the requisite know-how, and purchasing proprietary knowledge or third-party IP rights (subsection 37(4)). (As noted in Section 1.3, Budget 2026 proposes statutory carve-ins for initial commercialization regulatory testing and SR&ED-derived IP registration/maintenance outlays for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026).
3. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentives: Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryovers
3.1 Dual-Incentive Structure and Temporal Carryover Rules

Every valid federal SR&ED claim unlocks two complementary tax incentives under the Income Tax Act. First, under subsection 37(1), allowable current SR&ED expenditures and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) eligible ASA capital expenditures enter the cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Claimants may deduct up to 100% of this pool against net business income in the current taxation year, or elect to leave any portion undeducted and carry the pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future years.

Second, under section 127, the claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated on its year-end "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" (a single-year computation pool that does not carry over from year to year) at either the 15% basic rate or the 35% enhanced rate (computed as the 15% basic rate plus a 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1)). Where an SR&ED ITC is non-refundable (or exceeds current-year refundability limits), subsection 127(5) allows unused credits to be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years and carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable. Under subsection 127(5), the amount carried back to a prior year cannot exceed the lesser of (a) the portion of the current-year ITC that was not deductible against Part I tax in the current year, and (b) Part I tax otherwise payable in that prior year in excess of ITCs already available in that prior year. Any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash under section 127.1 is statutorily deemed to have been applied against Part I tax in the year, extinguishing it from carryback or carryforward availability.
3.2 Claimant Classifications: CCPCs, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and Other Entities
Entitlement to the 35% enhanced ITC rate and cash refundability depends strictly on the legal entity status and ownership control of the claimant throughout the taxation year.

Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs): Defined in subsection 125(7) of the Act, qualifying CCPCs have historically served as the primary beneficiaries of the enhanced SR&ED regime. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs earn the 35% enhanced ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their allocated share of the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit, and earn the 15% basic ITC on qualified expenditures exceeding that limit.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Enacted by Bill C-15 in subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an ECPC is a corporation that, throughout the taxation year, is resident in Canada, has a class of shares listed on a designated domestic or foreign stock exchange (such as the TSX, NYSE, or NASDAQ, or has elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation), and is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. As noted in PwC Canada's legislative analysis, Canadian-resident subsidiary corporations in which all or substantially all (90% or more) of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs also qualify for this enhanced refundable regime. This reform eliminates the longstanding "IPO penalty" under which Canadian technology and life-sciences firms immediately lost the 35% refundable credit upon listing publicly: qualifying ECPCs now earn the 35% enhanced ITC up to the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit and the 15% basic ITC on excess spending.

Foreign-Controlled Corporations, Large Public Corporations, Individuals, Partnerships, and Trusts: Corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs—most notably Canadian R&D subsidiaries controlled by foreign multinational parents, as well as public corporations phased out above $75 million in average gross revenue—earn the 15% basic ITC on an uncapped volume of qualified Canadian SR&ED expenditures, generally on a non-refundable basis. Unincorporated individuals (sole proprietors) and beneficiaries of trusts earn the 15% basic ITC. Under CRA's Get an investment tax credit guidance and published tax commentary on the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, individuals (and qualifying trusts/unincorporated structures) are eligible for a 40% cash refund of unclaimed basic ITCs after offsetting Part I tax. For partnerships, SR&ED claims are computed at the partnership level (SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy) and allocated to active partners under subsection 127(8) (excluding passive "specified members"), with partners of a partnership earning ITCs at the 15% basic rate rather than the 35% enhanced corporate rate.
3.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 maximum annual expenditure limit (generating up to $2,100,000 of enhanced ITC at 35%) must be shared across all associated CCPCs under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3) using T2 Schedule 49, or shared across all members of a consolidated group of ECPCs that prepare consolidated financial statements. If a corporation has a taxation year of less than 51 weeks, paragraph 127(10.5)(b) prorates its allocated expenditure limit by the ratio of days in the short taxation year to 365.

Federal law imposes no prior-year taxable income phase-out on the $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Instead, Bill C-15 provides two size-based phase-out mechanisms operating across an identical $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 range (reducing the $6,000,000 limit linearly across that $60,000,000 span—equivalent to a $1 limit reduction per $10, or 10%, of excess above $15,000,000 until reaching nil at $75,000,000).

Under the Taxable Capital Method (subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21)), which serves as the default rule for CCPCs, the $6,000,000 limit begins decreasing once the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (aggregated across all CCPCs in an associated group) reaches $15,000,000, and is eliminated completely at $75,000,000. Under the Gross Revenue Method (subsection 127(10.6)), which is mandatory for ECPCs, the $6,000,000 limit phases out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based on average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (determined from the consolidated financial statements of the group if the ECPC belongs to a consolidated group). Crucially, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a CCPC (or a group of associated CCPCs) may elect to determine its expenditure limit using this three-year average gross revenue formula instead of prior-year taxable capital. This election provides substantial relief to capital-intensive or venture-backed CCPCs whose balance-sheet capital exceeds $15 million (or even $75 million) while remaining early-revenue: when associated CCPCs elect under subsection 127(10.32), they sum the three-year average annual financial-statement revenues of every corporation that is a member of the group in the current tax year, regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout all three preceding years.
3.4 Refundability Matrix Under Section 127.1

Section 127.1 establishes distinct cash refundability rates depending on whether qualified expenditures are current (and PPA) versus capital, and whether a CCPC meets the legacy "qualifying corporation" test (10M–50M taxable capital grind reflected in CRA Glossary formulas). Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026) for CCPCs and tax practitioner analyses of Bill C-15 for ECPCs and other claimants (noting that Appendix A of the CRA policy governs granular non-CCPC tables), federal refundability operates as follows:

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Proxy vs. Traditional Election, and Restored Capital Rules
4.1 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and Permissible Foreign Labour

Employee remuneration is governed by subsection 248(1) and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025). Eligible SR&ED salary or wages must be paid to or incurred for employees in the taxation year (unpaid SR&ED expenditures are excluded from qualified expenditures in the year incurred under the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures Policy) and encompass employment income computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act—such as T4 gross wages—along with cash outlays for taxable benefits and qualifying non-cash taxable benefits (provided the benefit value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes GST/HST or PST unless no input tax credit is claimable, and the underlying cost is not also deducted as a regular business expense), bonuses and profit-based remuneration for non-specified employees, and qualifying employment inducements or non-competition payments.

Claimable employee roles depend on the overhead election: under the Proxy Method, only wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada qualify; under the Traditional Method, wages of employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED qualify as SR&ED wages, while wages of administrative employees directly attributable to SR&ED may be claimed on Line 360 as SR&ED overhead. In addition, under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), permissible salary or wages paid to employees performing SR&ED outside Canada qualify—capped at 10% of total directly engaged Canadian SR&ED salaries incurred in the year—provided the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer, relates to a business of the taxpayer, and is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer.

Strict statutory anti-avoidance caps govern "specified employees"—defined as any employee who is a "specified shareholder" owning, directly or indirectly or together with non-arm's-length persons, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the claimant or a related corporation, or who is related to (does not deal at arm's length with) a specified shareholder, such as a spouse or sibling. First, bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to specified employees are 100% excluded from SR&ED expenditures. Second, total allowable SR&ED salary or wages of a specified employee across an associated corporate group cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days in the year the individual was a specified employee. Associated corporations sharing a specified employee must file Form T1174 by their respective SR&ED reporting deadlines; failing to file Form T1174 on time deems the specified employee's SR&ED wages to be nil. Third, under subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) of the Regulations (Form T661, Lines 850 to 858), each specified employee's inclusion in the salary base for the 55% PPA is capped at the lesser of: (a) directly engaged SR&ED salary (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits); (b) 75% of total annual salary or wages (SR&ED plus non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits); and (c) 2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, prorated by days employed in the year (2.5 × YMPE × Days Employed ÷ 365, with no proration for days the individual was not a specified employee). body.text: 4.2 Overhead Methodologies (Proxy 55% vs. Traditional) and Cloud/Software Treatment

Claimants must elect either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method on Form T661 to treat SR&ED overhead and other expenditures for the taxation year. Under the Proxy Method (Regulation 2900(4)), chosen by the majority of Canadian claimants, overhead outlays are not tracked or included in the section 37 SR&ED pool (remaining deductible as ordinary business expenses). Instead, for ITC calculation purposes on Line 820 of Form T661, the claimant adds a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of its eligible SR&ED salary base (note: as CPA guidance highlights, the PPA was 65% up to 2012 and 60% in 2013, and has stood at 55% since 2014; using 65% overstates every claim). Only directly engaged Canadian SR&ED employee salaries (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits, and capped for specified employees) enter the PPA base—subcontractor invoices never generate PPA, and the PPA is subject to an overall statutory expense cap.

Under the Traditional Method (Regulation 2900, Line 360 of Form T661), no PPA is claimed; instead, the claimant specifically identifies, tracks, allocates, and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and incremental (meaning they would not have been incurred had SR&ED not been performed), such as incremental shop maintenance, SR&ED travel and training, property taxes, directly attributable administrative salaries, and qualifying sub-90% equipment lease costs. Traditional overhead enters both the section 37 deduction pool and the section 127 ITC pool, making the Traditional Method advantageous where actual incremental facility or equipment operating expenses exceed 55% of directly engaged payroll.

With respect to cloud computing and software costs, CRA's published policy inventory does not contain a standalone cloud-computing circular; instead, software and cloud outlays are governed by general statutory rules across sections 37 and 127 and CRA's overhead, materials, and capital policies. Specifically, expenditures to acquire rights in or arising out of SR&ED (subsection 37(4)) or to purchase off-the-shelf proprietary knowledge are ineligible, and intangible software or data subscriptions do not constitute physical "materials consumed or transformed". Consequently, non-capital operational outlays (such as incremental compute or software usage directly related and incremental to SR&ED experimentation in Canada) are implicitly absorbed within the 55% PPA when electing the Proxy Method, or must be specifically tracked and substantiated as directly related and incremental SR&ED overhead on Line 360 when electing the Traditional Method (while post-December 15, 2024 acquisitions or leases of physical servers/hardware follow the restored capital and lease rules below).
4.3 Materials Consumed or Transformed, Subcontractors, and Third-Party Payments

Under both the Proxy and Traditional Methods, three direct current expenditure streams are claimed separately. Materials for SR&ED (Materials for SR&ED Policy) are 100% deductible under section 37 and 100% eligible for the SR&ED ITC, encompassing materials consumed (rendered virtually valueless during experimentation) and materials transformed (incorporated into another medium or prototype during SR&ED, subject to ITC recapture under subsection 127(27) if later sold or converted to commercial use).

Arm's-length contract expenditures (Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy) paid for SR&ED performed on the claimant's behalf in Canada are 100% deductible in the section 37 pool, but under subsection 127(9) only 80% of the eligible contract amount qualifies for the SR&ED ITC. Crucially, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" (a Canadian-resident person, Canadian partnership, or non-resident operating through a Canadian permanent establishment) performing the SR&ED work inside Canada; offshore subcontractor work earns zero ITC. Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length (NAL) party, contract payments are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures; instead, the NAL performer either claims its underlying SR&ED costs directly (deemed SR&ED under section 37) or transfers qualified expenditures to the NAL payer via Form T1146 (with related assistance allocated via Form T1145). Similarly, third-party payments (Form T1263, Third-Party Payments Policy) made under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii) to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, or paragraph 149(1)(j) tax-exempt research corporations for SR&ED related to the claimant's business (where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results) are 100% deductible under section 37 and 80% eligible for the SR&ED ITC.
4.4 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and ITC Recapture

Under Bill C-15 and the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), depreciable capital equipment and lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024 once again qualify for SR&ED incentives.

All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) Capital Expenditures (Line 390 of Form T661): Expenditures to acquire new or used depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualify at 100% for both the section 37 deduction pool and the section 127 ITC pool (with the enhanced 35% ITC on capital being 40% refundable in cash) if, at acquisition, the claimant intended either to use the asset all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time across its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume 90% or more of its value performing SR&ED in Canada. ASA capital claimed on Line 390 must not be included on T2 Schedule 8 for Capital Cost Allowance (CCA). Claimants must list up to the 10 most expensive ASA properties on Line 262, enter their SR&ED operating-time percentages on Line 263, and report related capital assistance, prescribed expenditures, deductions, and NAL transfers on Lines 518, 532, 535, and 540. Non-depreciable property (such as land), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are strictly excluded from ASA capital expenditures (note: while one CPA blog summary mentions leasehold interests differently, official CRA instructions on canada.ca explicitly state that "Non-depreciable assets, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are not eligible SR&ED capital expenditures", and statutory text in subparagraph 37(8)(e)(iv) likewise restricts payments enabling recipients to acquire buildings or leasehold interests in buildings).

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Line 504 of Form T661): Where new depreciable equipment (excluding used equipment and "prescribed depreciable property" such as buildings or equipment intended primarily for non-SR&ED over its useful life) is acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 and does not meet the 90% ASA test, it qualifies for SUE ITCs (identically under both Proxy and Traditional Methods) if used primarily (more than 50% of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada across two statutory periods: 25% of capital cost qualifies as First-Term SUE at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition/availability for use, and a second 25% qualifies as Second-Term SUE in the subsequent period. SUE capital cost does not enter the section 37 pool; instead, it is depreciated via regular CCA on T2 Schedule 8, and up to the 20 most expensive SUE assets must be named on Form T661.

Equipment Lease Expenditures and Recapture: Lease outlays incurred or first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 for equipment qualify at 100% if meeting the 90% ASA test. Where leased equipment (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture) is used less than 90% in SR&ED, lease costs are covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method, whereas under the Traditional Method they are claimable on Line 360—including 50% (one-half) of current lease outlays for equipment used primarily (>50% to <90%) in SR&ED in Canada under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI). Finally, if SR&ED capital property, SUE, or transformed materials are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, recapture rules (subsections 127(27) to 127(36) and Line 440 CCA recapture) apply to recover previously claimed SR&ED tax benefits.

body.text: 5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal-Provincial Stacking
5.1 Government Assistance Grinding and Worked Stacking Calculations

Nine Canadian provinces and Yukon administer R&D tax credits that stack with federal SR&ED incentives, whereas Prince Edward Island, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut offer no provincial or territorial R&D credit. Under subsections 127(18) to 127(20) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—alongside government grants, non-government assistance, and contract payments received, receivable, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing-due date—constitute assistance that reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar. Under section 4.5 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, when a claimant uses the Proxy Method, the entire provincial R&D tax credit (whether refundable or non-refundable, including the portion earned on the notional 55% PPA) reduces federal qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18); however, because the notional PPA is not in the section 37 deductible pool, the PPA-attributable portion of the provincial credit does not reduce the section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) and must instead be included directly in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received.

body.text: 5.2 Québec's Structural Overhaul: The CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025) vs. Legacy Credits

Administered independently by Revenu Québec, Québec enacted a fundamental structural overhaul in its March 25, 2025 budget: for taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec replaced its suite of legacy R&D credits with the fully refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation, administered under Codes 112 and 113, alongside Form RD-222-V for R&D expenditure deductions).

Under official Revenu Québec and Ministère des Finances du Québec guidance, the CRIC is restricted strictly to qualified corporations and corporations that are members of a qualified partnership carrying out innovation projects in Québec—unincorporated individuals and specified members of partnerships are no longer eligible. Crucially, the CRIC expands eligible activities beyond traditional R&D to subsidize pre-commercialization activities—including tests, technological validations, studies carried out to satisfy regulatory requirements, and product design—provided those activities constitute a continuation of R&D undertaken in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation or partnership in respect of its business. Eligible Québec expenditures across both R&D and pre-commercialization cover salaries and wages, subcontractor payments, payments to eligible research organizations, and capital expenditures to acquire depreciable property.

To focus assistance on substantive R&D teams, eligible expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and pre-commercialization employees threshold. Expenditures exceeding that exclusion threshold earn a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible spending—regardless of the corporation's asset size (shared among associated corporations, per accounting firm budget summaries)—and a 20% refundable rate on all eligible spending above $1,000,000. (Québec also maintains a 2% effective corporate tax rate on qualified IP taxable income, and Québec's nexus ratio is not reduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold).

For taxation years or fiscal periods beginning before March 26, 2025, claimants continue to file Québec's four legacy credits (whose detailed historical rate tables are published in Revenu Québec guide IN-109-V):

items: Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V and Form RD-222-V);
Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V and Form RD-222-V);
Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V, Form RD-222-V, and a mandatory qualification certificate from the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy); and

Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V), under which cumulative fee balances from taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025 remain claimable under transitional rules for taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029.

body.text: 5.3 Ontario's Three-Tier R&D Suite (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) for corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment that file a timely federal Form T661, Ontario operates three stackable corporate R&D credits. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule 566, Schedule 5 Line 468) provides an 8% refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures plus eligible repayments (up to $240,000 annually, shared across associated corporations and prorated for short tax years). Notably, Ontario aligned with federal capital restoration—including 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (while excluding capital made between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024)—but kept its $3,000,000 expenditure cap and dual phase-out grinds unchanged. Specifically, the $3,000,000 OITC limit phases out linearly if prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000, and phases out linearly if prior-year taxable/specified capital in Canada lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 (multiplying the two survival percentages when both grinds apply, as illustrated in Ontario CPA analyses), and may be waived in whole or in part under subsection 96(14).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508, Schedule 5 Line 416) provides an uncapped 3.5% non-refundable credit (4.5% before June 1, 2016) on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (less any OITC claimed), carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. Third, as detailed in Ontario tax guidance, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 and 569, Schedule 5 Line 470) provides a 20% refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures under eligible contracts with qualifying Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence (up to $4,000,000 cash annually).
5.4 Western, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

Across Western Canada, Alberta administers its standalone Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) via Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970, due 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date), providing a 100% refundable credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending at an 8% base rate up to the corporation's prior two-year average Alberta R&D spend and an enhanced 20% rate on incremental spending above that two-year base. British Columbia (Form T666, due 18 months after corporate tax year-end) provides a 10% refundable credit for CCPCs up to $3,000,000 ($300,000 max) and a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward) above $3 million and for other corporations. Saskatchewan (T2 Schedule 403) provides CCPCs a 10% refundable credit up to $1,000,000 ($100,000 max) and a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward) above $1 million and for non-CCPCs. Manitoba (T2 Schedule 380, due 1 year after the filing-due date) provides a 15% credit that is half refundable (7.5% refundable / 7.5% non-refundable, 3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward) for in-house R&D and 100% refundable (15%) for contract R&D with qualifying institutes.

In Atlantic and Northern Canada, New Brunswick (T2 Schedule 360), Nova Scotia (due 18 months after corporate tax year-end), and Newfoundland and Labrador (T2 Schedule 301 for corporations; Form T1129 for individuals; due 12 months after the filing-due date) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit (with NB carrying legacy non-refundable rules of 3 years back / 7 years forward). Yukon (T2 Schedule 442 for corporations; Form T1232 for individuals; due 12 months after the filing-due date) provides a 15% refundable credit plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.

body.text: 6. Administration, Optional Pre-Claim Approval, Compliance Deadlines, and Program Empirical Trends
6.1 Mandatory Statutory Filing Deadlines and Updated 2026 Prescribed Forms

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a claimant must file prescribed forms (Form T661 plus T2 Schedule 31 for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals) containing all prescribed information on or before the day that is one year (12 months) after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the particular year. For corporations, this establishes an absolute statutory reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, June 30, 2027 for a December 31, 2025 year-end). There is no statutory mechanism to extend this deadline: if a claim is filed late, or if the CRA notifies a claimant of missing prescribed information on an incomplete claim and the claimant fails to submit the missing items before the SR&ED reporting deadline expires, the CRA cannot accept additional information and the claimed SR&ED expenditures and ITCs are permanently forfeited. Following Royal Assent of Bill C-15, the CRA updated its suite of prescribed forms and interpretive policies across 2026:

body.text: 6.2 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Launched on April 1, 2026, the CRA's Optional Pre-Claim Approval program enables businesses to confirm technical project eligibility before beginning SR&ED work (or shortly after starting) and before incurring major costs. Eligible applicants must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership in good standing with the CRA with gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and the proposed project must not have been included in a prior SR&ED claim or involve issues currently under litigation. (Free one-on-one pre-claim information sessions are also available through OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca, alongside the SR&ED Client Portal and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool inside My Business Account).
The Pre-Claim Approval workflow executes in four sequential steps:

items: Confirm business and project eligibility and request a case number from the CRA;

Complete the structured technical application (addressing the baseline state of technology, the scientific or technological uncertainty, planned hypotheses, and experimental methodology) and compile supporting documentation;

Upload the complete application via My Business Account, triggering assignment of a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—for existing SR&ED claimants in good standing, an RTA meeting is optional, whereas for all other businesses a 2- to 5-hour technical meeting with the RTA (including a company technical expert and optional virtual or on-site facility tour, concluding with a verbal RTA summary) is mandatory; and
Receive a formal written CRA Pre-Claim Approval determination within 8 weeks of submitting a complete application, then file the standard year-end Form T661 SR&ED claim after fiscal year-end.

body.text: 6.3 CRA Processing Standards, Audit Selection, and Multi-Year Program Statistics (2021–2026)

CRA processing service standards are set out as follows (there is no service standard for non-refundable claims selected for review): 60 days for all claims accepted as filed; 90 days for refundable claims selected for review that only contain projects granted Pre-Claim Approval; and 180 days for refundable claims selected for review that include any project without Pre-Claim Approval or materially differing from its pre-approved scope. First-time claimants—or claimants that have not filed an SR&ED claim in the preceding 3 years—may be selected for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service, while claims selected for compliance review are examined by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and a Financial Reviewer (FR), backed by the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025).

7. Judicial Precedents, Contemporaneous Documentation, and Dispute Resolution
7.1 Controlling Jurisprudence: Northwest Hydraulic, Kam-Press Metal Products, and Appellate Rulings

Judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) is anchored in Judge Bowman's landmark Tax Court of Canada ruling in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (1998), which is incorporated directly into the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors. Synthesized with CRA eligibility guidelines and appellate rulings, the five-part Northwest Hydraulic framework examines: (1) whether there was a scientific or technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; (2) whether the claimant formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; (3) "whether the procedure adopted accord[ed] with the total discipline of the scientific method", including formulating, testing, and modifying hypotheses; (4) whether the process resulted in a scientific or technological advancement; and (5) whether detailed contemporaneous records of the hypotheses tested and experimental results were kept as the work progressed.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada), 2021 FCA 88, the taxpayer argued that because subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act contains no literal reference to the words "scientific method", the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion should not be imposed. As tax counsel at Thorsteinssons LLP and Canadian Lawyer report, the Federal Court of Appeal squarely rejected that argument, affirming that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria represent the settled legal interpretation of subsection 248(1). In May 2022, a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal written by Justice Rennie reaffirmed Kam-Press in dismissing a consulting firm's SR&ED appeal, holding that post-hoc expert testimony could not rescue a claim where the taxpayer failed to work methodically and where its records were "vague," "unclear," and failed to reflect "a logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result". Similarly, as Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt LLP notes regarding National R&D Inc., pursuing commercial cost efficiency is relevant to SR&ED only where overcoming underlying technological uncertainty is required rather than routine optimization.
7.2 Contemporaneous Documentation Standards and Dispute Resolution Pathway

Because larger refundable claims under Bill C-15's $6,000,000 cap and restored capital rules will attract heightened CRA audit scrutiny, claimants must maintain contemporaneous technical and financial records generated naturally during R&D execution—linking initial technological uncertainties, dated hypotheses, test data, failed iterations, employee time allocations, Canadian taxable-supplier subcontractor invoices, and post-December 15, 2024 capital/SUE operating-time logs (Lines 262, 263, 390, and 504) directly to the general ledger.
Where a claimant disagrees with proposed or assessed adjustments following a CRA claim review, four sequential remedies govern dispute resolution:

items: Direct Reviewer Engagement: Present clarifying contemporaneous technical and financial documentation directly to the assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and/or Financial Reviewer (FR) during the review;

Managerial Administrative Review (Form RC532): If concerns remain unresolved with frontline reviewers, escalate to the Research and Technology Manager and/or Financial Review Manager under the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns;
Formal Notice of Objection: File a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment; and

Judicial Appeal: If the claimant disagrees with the CRA's decision on the objection, file a judicial appeal to the Tax Court of Canada, with further appellate review on questions of law available before the Federal Court of Appeal.
